results.name: mixed_parity_range_gap
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples mixing odd and even numbers, yes rate for targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus targets outside it; observed above null means people use the example range more sharply than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: mixed_parity_range_gap
# description: In sets of >=2 examples mixing odd and even numbers, yes rate for targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus targets outside it; observed above null means people use the example range more sharply than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    mixed = (n >= 2) & (np.nanmax(par, axis=1) != np.nanmin(par, axis=1))
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    inside = (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    return rate(mixed & inside) - rate(mixed & ~inside)

results.name: singleton_distance_gradient
results.description: For single-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding it) minus targets more than 30 away; observed above null means a steeper similarity gradient for one example than the model predicts, below means flatter.
results.code:
# name: singleton_distance_gradient
# description: For single-example sets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding it) minus targets more than 30 away; observed above null means a steeper similarity gradient for one example than the model predicts, below means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    s = (n == 1)
    d = np.abs(t - ex[:, 0])
    return rate(s & (d >= 1) & (d <= 10)) - rate(s & (d > 30))

results.name: recency_last_vs_first_example
results.description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets within 10 of the first or last-shown example, yes rate when the target is closer to the last example minus closer to the first; observed above null means a recency effect the order-blind model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: recency_last_vs_first_example
# description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets within 10 of the first or last-shown example, yes rate when the target is closer to the last example minus closer to the first; observed above null means a recency effect the order-blind model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    idx = np.clip(n - 1, 0, None).astype(int)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(t)), idx]
    df_ = np.abs(t - first); dl = np.abs(t - last)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (dmin >= 1) & (np.minimum(df_, dl) <= 10) & (first != last)
    return rate(base & (dl < df_)) - rate(base & (df_ < dl))

results.name: final_digit_match_gap
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples all sharing a final digit, yes rate for targets with that final digit minus targets without; observed above null means people pick up final-digit rules more strongly than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: final_digit_match_gap
# description: In sets of >=2 examples all sharing a final digit, yes rate for targets with that final digit minus targets without; observed above null means people pick up final-digit rules more strongly than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    fd = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 10)
    same = (n >= 2) & (np.nanmax(fd, axis=1) == np.nanmin(fd, axis=1))
    match = (t % 10) == np.nanmin(fd, axis=1)
    return rate(same & match) - rate(same & ~match)

results.name: near_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets within 1-3 of the nearest example (but not an example itself); observed above null means the model under-generalizes to close neighbours (too little similarity gradient), below means it over-generalizes.

    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()

    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)

results.name: above_vs_below_range_asymmetry
results.description: Yes rate for targets 1-20 above the largest example minus targets 1-20 below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend generalization upward more than the symmetric-interval model predicts, below means downward.
results.code:
# name: above_vs_below_range_asymmetry
# description: Yes rate for targets 1-20 above the largest example minus targets 1-20 below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend generalization upward more than the symmetric-interval model predicts, below means downward.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1), np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    above = (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 20)
    below = (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 20)
    return rate(above) - rate(below)

results.name: parity_match_gap_large_sets
results.description: In sets of >=3 examples that are all even or all odd, yes rate for targets of matching parity minus mismatching parity; observed above null means people rely on parity more than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_gap_large_sets
# description: In sets of >=3 examples that are all even or all odd, yes rate for targets of matching parity minus mismatching parity; observed above null means people rely on parity more than the model, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    def rate(mask):
        return float(r[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    same = (n >= 3) & (np.nanmax(par, axis=1) == np.nanmin(par, axis=1))
    p0 = np.nanmin(par, axis=1)
    match = (t % 2) == p0
    return rate(same & match) - rate(same & ~match)
